mainEntity.name: If my neighbor's tree falls on my fence, who pays in Michigan?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually you do, through your own homeowners policy. Michigan treats a healthy tree that fails in a storm as an act of God, so the tree's owner is not automatically liable. If the tree was visibly hazardous and the owner knew — dead limbs, trunk cracks, a worsening lean — the owner may be liable, and written notice from you to them makes that case much stronger.

mainEntity.name: Does homeowners insurance cover a fence blown down by wind?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually yes, under Coverage B, the other-structures section of your policy, typically limited to about 10% of your dwelling coverage. Wind, hail, fire, vandalism, vehicle impact, and a healthy tree falling on the fence are all commonly covered. Rot, termites, neglect, and flood are not.

mainEntity.name: How much will insurance actually pay for a 15-year-old wood fence?

acceptedAnswer.text: Less than you expect. Wood fences are usually settled at actual cash value, so the adjuster depreciates for age and condition before subtracting your deductible. On a $9,900 fence with 60% depreciation and a $2,500 deductible, the check is about $1,460 — which is why many homeowners with older fences choose to pay for the repair themselves.

mainEntity.name: Should I file a claim for a fence repair?

acceptedAnswer.text: Only if the repair costs meaningfully more than your deductible. If the estimate is below your deductible, filing pays you nothing and still puts a claim on your loss history. If it is several times the deductible, file promptly, because prompt notice is a condition of coverage.

mainEntity.name: How long do I have to file a homeowners claim in Michigan?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no fixed day count for notice — the policy requires prompt notice, and delay that prejudices the insurer can jeopardize coverage. The harder deadlines are: the insurer must tell you in writing within 30 days what proof of loss it needs (MCL 500.2006), payment is due within 60 days of satisfactory proof or 12% interest accrues, and the deadline to sue is at least one year from the loss (MCL 500.2833).

mainEntity.name: Can I trim branches from my neighbor's tree that hang over my fence?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, up to the property line, under Michigan's self-help rule, and you pay for it yourself. You cannot reach past the line or step onto their property without permission, and you cannot cut so aggressively that you kill or seriously damage the tree. Cutting a neighbor's tree without permission exposes you to treble damages under MCL 600.2919.

mainEntity.name: What if the tree trunk sits right on the property line?

acceptedAnswer.text: Michigan treats it as jointly owned. Under Lennon v. Terrall, 250 Mich. 100 (1932), neither owner may cut, injure, or destroy a boundary tree without the other's consent, and maintenance is shared. Get any agreement in writing before a saw shows up.

mainEntity.name: Do I need a permit to repair a storm-damaged fence in Oakland County?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually not for a like-for-like repair of a few damaged sections, but most cities do require a permit for a new or fully replaced run, and the rules differ by municipality. Check with your city's building department, and see our city-by-city fence rules guide for the height, setback, and permit requirements in your community.

mainEntity.name: Is it cheaper to repair the damaged sections or replace the whole fence?

acceptedAnswer.text: Repair wins on a fence under 12 years old with sound posts — replace the two damaged bays and move on. Replacement wins when more than about 30% of the posts are compromised, when the fence is beyond its service life, or when the repair cost approaches 40% of a new run. We measure posts before we quote either way.
